'''John E. Hearst''' (July 3, 1935 – October 25, 2022) was an American-Austrian chemist in the fields of [[chemistry]] and [[molecular biology]] and a Professor Emeritus at [[University of California Berkeley]].<ref name=berkeley>{{Cite web|url=http://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/emeriti/hearst|title=John Hearst &#124; College of Chemistry}}</ref> He is known for his scientific work in [[molecular biology]], especially in [[DNA]] modeling.

==Biography==
Hearst was born in [[Vienna]], [[Austria]] on July 2, 1935, and immigrated to the United States as a small child to escape the Nazi regime.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hoge |first=Patrick |date=2005-01-26 |title=Lily Hearst, 107 -- Berkeley's oldest citizen |url=https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/Lily-Hearst-107-Berkeley-s-oldest-citizen-2735566.php |access-date=2022-10-09 |website=SFGATE |language=en-US}}</ref> He completed his B.E. from Yale University in 1957 followed by a Ph.D. from the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1961. His advisor was the well-known molecular biologist Prof. Jonathan Singer. He became a Miller Professor at Berkeley in 1970 followed by an illuminated career in science and scientific leadership,<ref name=berkeley/> among other key appointments serving as the Senior Staff Scientist, Structural Biology Division, [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] (1980–1999), and as the director of the Chemical Biodynamics Division, Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory for two terms (1986–1987, 1988–1989). He served as a president of the [[American Society for Photobiology]] (1991–1992).

In the 1970s he worked with his collaborated with his colleague Henry Rapport developing a photochemical method of inactivation of pathogens that became the basis for the work of HRI Research and HRI Associates and later the [[Cerus Corporation]], which he co-founded in 1991.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Henry Rapoport {{!}} College of Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/henry-rapoport |access-date=2022-10-09 |website=chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref> As founding director, he served on the board of directors for a decade (1991–2003). He continued on as vice president of new science opportunities until his retirement in 2004 when he transitioned into a consulting role.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cerus Corporation Announces Transition of John Hearst |url=https://ir.cerus.com/press-releases/press-releases-details/2004/Cerus-Corporation-Announces-Transition-of-John-Hearst/default.aspx |access-date=2022-10-09 |website=ir.cerus.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 

He advised a number of graduate students during his career and led the Hearst Research Laboratory/group at Berkeley till his retirement.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/jehgrp/|title = Hearst Group Home Page}}</ref> He has a high number of citations to his work (20,520) and an [[h-index]] of 74.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3691TcwAAAAJ&hl=en|title=John e. Hearst}}</ref> He was also an author of a book on general chemistry.

Hearst was awarded an honorary degree of D.Sc. by [[Lehigh University]] in 1992. He was a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and a  [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]] in 1968.<ref name=berkeley/><ref name="Guggenheim">{{cite web |title=John E. Hearst |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/john-e-hearst/ |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation... |access-date=22 May 2023}}</ref>

Hearst died on October 25, 2022, at the age of 87.<ref name="obit">{{cite web |title=In Memoriam: John E. Hearst |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/memoriam-john-e-hearst |website=Berkeley College of Chemistry |access-date=22 May 2023 |date=October 25, 2022}}</ref>
